profile.title: Prediabetes and Anemia Follow-up Nutrition Counseling in a 33-Year-Old Caregiver Experiencing Maintenance Relapse
profile.summary: This case portrays a 33-year-old caregiver with prediabetes (rising HbA1c) and iron-deficiency anemia whose highly agreeable, deflecting communication style masks a quiet relapse from an earlier period of successful self-management. It trains dietetics students to look past verbal agreement to actual behavior, uncover household and caregiving barriers to dietary change through rapport-building, and spot a patient-versus-record mismatch (stated daily iron adherence versus a pharmacy refill record showing inconsistent fills) while negotiating one small, sustainable change rather than a full overhaul.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Orange, New Jersey, seated in her kitchen with occasional background noise from her mother-in-law's room

patient.name: Margarita Emmerich
patient.occupation: Currently unemployed; previously a dental hygienist before leaving her job to care for her husband's mother
patient.appearance: Appears tired with faint dark circles under her eyes, conjunctiva slightly pale on close video inspection; sits in a tidy kitchen, phone nearby that she checks frequently as if waiting for a message; shifts in her chair occasionally, wincing slightly and rubbing her lower back; dressed neatly, warm and quick to smile.

persona.personality: Warm, eager to please, highly agreeable — she affirms suggestions readily ('Yes, absolutely, that makes sense') but rarely pushes back or admits when something won't work for her. Deflects personal questions with a question of her own.
persona.communicationStyle: Articulate and above-average health literacy from her own research and dental hygiene background; uses some technical terms correctly (e.g., glycemic index, iron absorption). Tends to answer 'how are you doing' with vague reassurance ('pretty much the same as always') and turns questions back on the clinician rather than giving direct personal detail.
persona.emotionalState: Outwardly upbeat and cooperative, but visibly tired (dark circles, pale conjunctiva on close look, frequent phone-checking) with an undercurrent of worry she downplays when asked directly about stress.
persona.background: Margarita is a 33-year-old former dental hygienist in Orange, New Jersey, who left her job in 2022 to help care for her husband's mother, who moved in with them that year. She grew up believing the kitchen belongs to whichever woman is most senior in the household, so she doesn't feel it's her place to direct what's cooked or how it's portioned. Her closest support is her neighbor Denise, who checks in several times a week and used to walk with her in the evenings. She keeps a running list of nutrition articles saved on her phone she rarely has time to act on, and tends a small herb pot on the windowsill — one of the few food-related things that's entirely hers.
speechExamples: Yes, absolutely, that makes a lot of sense — I should probably do that.
Things have been pretty good, pretty much the same as always, honestly.
What would you do if you were in my situation, though?
I read that pairing iron with vitamin C helps absorption, right? I try to remember that.
Oh, I just eat what's put in front of me — that's kind of how it's always been in this house.
concerns: Worried the prediabetes will progress to full diabetes like it did for her aunt
Concerned her anemia is making the caregiving harder on her
Afraid she's losing the progress she made a couple of years ago

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit with Margarita Emmerich, a 33-year-old woman being followed for prediabetes and anemia. She was flagged on recent labs for blood sugar and iron trending in the wrong direction. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment and provide patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing. You do not yet know the details of her home situation, her actual eating pattern, or how consistently she is following prior recommendations — you'll need to draw these out.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up for prediabetes and anemia; labs show blood sugar and iron trending the wrong way since she last made progress on her diet about two years ago.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me again — they told me my blood sugar's kind of borderline now and my iron's a little low, but honestly things have been pretty good, pretty much the same as always.
tasks: Take a focused nutrition and diet history, including who prepares and controls meals in the household
Review relevant anthropometric and laboratory trends with the patient to understand how her status has changed over time
Assess physical activity history and any recent changes
Clarify current supplement use and routine, comparing what the patient reports with available records
Identify one small, realistic, caregiver-compatible change to co-create with the patient using motivational interviewing, and document findings in ADIME format

objectives.text: Elicit a focused diet history that identifies who actually prepares, plans, and portions meals in the household, and how this shapes the patient's real dietary intake.
Review anthropometric and laboratory trends over time (weight/BMI, HbA1c, hemoglobin) to characterize the trajectory of glycemic and iron status rather than relying on a single value.
Assess current and past physical activity patterns to identify a lapsed routine and the barriers (caregiving guilt, chronic back pain) contributing to its decline.
Clarify actual supplement adherence by comparing the patient's self-report with pharmacy refill records, and connect findings such as pagophagia to possible ongoing iron deficiency.
Recognize how an agreeable, deflecting communication style and caregiving burden can mask lack of behavior change, and build rapport to surface hidden stress and sleep disruption.

Apply motivational interviewing principles to co-create one small, caregiver-compatible nutrition or activity change that respects household dynamics, leveraging existing supports such as her neighbor Denise.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Prediabetes (HbA1c 5.9%, trending up from a lower baseline two years ago) and persistent iron-deficiency anemia (Hgb 11.9 g/dL) in the context of inconsistent dietary control, lapsed physical activity, and probable inconsistent iron supplement adherence, occurring during a maintenance-to-relapse shift driven by unacknowledged caregiving burden.
differential: Excess intake of refined starches/added sugars relative to needs contributing to rising HbA1c
Inadequate dietary iron and vitamin-C pairing plus inconsistent supplement adherence contributing to persistent anemia
Insufficient physical activity (lapsed walking routine) contributing to weight gain and glycemic trend
Psychosocial/caregiving stress and sleep disruption affecting self-care capacity and reinforcing an all-or-nothing change belief
Low self-perceived control over household meal planning limiting ability to implement dietary changes
keyFindings: HbA1c 5.9% (up from an earlier, better value ~2022-2023), fasting glucose 96 mg/dL
Hgb 11.9 g/dL (ref 12.0-17.5), with pagophagia (ice craving) reported as 'odd' but unconnected by patient
Diet entirely planned/cooked/plated by mother-in-law; low vegetable consistency, frequent refined-starch breakfasts (toast/pastry)
Previously walked 30 min evenings with neighbor Denise; has quietly stopped over several months
Sleep 6 hours or less, interrupted overnight by caregiving duties; patient minimizes stress when asked directly
Patient states she takes her iron supplement 'every day like I'm supposed to,' but pharmacy refill record shows only 2 of the last 6 monthly fills (patient-vs-chart mismatch)
Highly agreeable communication style ('yes, absolutely') with vague follow-through and frequent deflection via counter-questions
plan: Complete nutrition assessment (ADIME) including diet history, 24-hour recall anchored to actual meals cooked by mother-in-law, and anthropometric trend review
Clarify actual iron supplement adherence by reviewing pharmacy refill pattern and reconciling with patient's stated adherence; discuss pagophagia as a possible sign of ongoing iron deficiency

Negotiate one small, caregiver-compatible nutrition change (e.g., adding a vitamin-C-paired iron-rich side at dinner, or a lower-glycemic-index breakfast swap she can source herself) rather than a full overhaul
Explore re-engaging neighbor Denise for short, guilt-manageable walks as a step toward restoring prior activity level
Use motivational interviewing to gently surface the gap between stated agreement and actual follow-through, and to validate caregiving strain without pathologizing it
Document nutrition diagnosis and plan in ADIME format; schedule follow-up to recheck HbA1c and hemoglobin trend and reassess adherence
Encourage non-confrontational strategies for requesting small meal adjustments that preserve respect for mother-in-law's role in the kitchen
redFlags: Worsening anemia trend with pagophagia could indicate ongoing or worsening iron deficiency warranting medical/lab follow-up beyond nutrition counseling
Rising HbA1c trajectory toward diabetes range if current pattern continues
Caregiver burnout risk given minimal sleep, no personal time in four months, and reluctance to disclose stress
educationPoints: Explain how pairing iron-rich foods with vitamin C sources (e.g., citrus she already likes) can improve absorption
Explain in plain terms what the HbA1c number means and why the trend (not just the single value) matters
Clarify that small, sustainable changes (e.g., one swapped breakfast item or short walks) are more realistic and effective than an all-or-nothing overhaul, especially given caregiving demands
Discuss that occasional ice craving can be a sign of low iron and is worth tracking rather than dismissing as odd
Reinforce that asking for small meal adjustments at home does not have to mean criticizing or taking over her mother-in-law's cooking

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports taking iron supplement daily as prescribed since 2022 diagnosis (h6/s16)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows only 2 of the last 6 monthly iron supplement fills, with the most recent fill over 2 months ago (d5)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Stated adherence should be cross-checked against objective records like pharmacy refill history; discrepancies may explain persistent lab abnormalities such as unresolved anemia, and should be explored non-judgmentally rather than taken at face value.
